sentence: I left my umbrella, a good umbrella, a reliable umbrella, on the train. I have done this so many times that I have begun to think of it less as losing umbrellas and more as gently donating them, one by one, to the railway network, a slow and unintentional act of charity. Somewhere there is a lost property office containing a small museum of my former umbrellas, each one a monument to a journey on which I did not, quite, remember everything.

I made a curry from scratch last weekend. I bought twelve different spices. I toasted them. I ground them. I sweated onions for forty minutes. I followed a recipe by a chef whose face was on the cover of three different food magazines. The final dish tasted, identifiably, like the takeaway curry from the place around the corner. The takeaway curry costs nine pounds. The takeaway curry takes twenty minutes. I have learned an expensive lesson.

Walking down a crowded city street in the rain is a slow, perilous fencing match conducted entirely with umbrellas. Everyone holds their umbrella at a slightly different height, and so the tall person's umbrella jousts with the short person's umbrella, spokes interlock, apologies are mumbled, and the entire pavement becomes a low-speed collision of nylon domes, everyone soaked anyway, the umbrellas having achieved nothing but a kind of communal, dripping chaos.

subtopic: humour about work, tech, or science
sentence: Two physicists walk into a bar. The first one says, 'I'll have a glass of H2O.' The second one says, 'I'll have a glass of H2O too.' The second physicist dies. This joke has been doing the rounds in physics departments for forty years, which tells you everything you need to know about the dating prospects of physicists.

subtopic: humour about work, tech, or science
sentence: Every meeting could have been an email, every email could have been a Slack message, and every Slack message could have been left unsent for the rest of human history with no measurable impact on the productivity of our species. And yet here we are, on a call about a call we had last Thursday, scheduling a follow-up call. The capitalism is calling from inside the house.

The best man's speech began with the words 'I'll keep this brief' and continued, against all known laws of time, for twenty-six minutes. He told a story about a stag do that I am fairly sure was a criminal confession. He referenced four in-jokes that nobody in the room understood, including, judging by his face, the groom. He cried twice. We clapped, eventually, out of relief rather than appreciation, and the relief was genuine and deep.

subtopic: humour about work, tech, or science
sentence: Our company values, written in huge letters on the lobby wall, are Innovation, Integrity, and Impact. The first one means the coffee machine is broken. The second one means somebody stole my lunch and lied about it. The third one means we are now hiring a Chief Vibes Officer, whose job is to issue motivational quotes via the office Slack channel that nobody opens.

The password field showed my password as a row of small dots, hiding it for my own protection, in case a spy was reading over my shoulder. There was no spy. There is never a spy. I am alone, in my kitchen, at night. But the website does not know this, and so it hides my password from me, the one person who is desperately, urgently trying to see it, while protecting it from a watcher who does not, and has never, existed.

I have reached step fourteen of the assembly instructions and discovered that step fourteen requires a part I attached, irreversibly, during step six. To proceed, I must go back. To go back, I must undo six panels, four dowels, and my own sense of progress. I sat on the floor for a while, among the wooden pieces, and considered my life. Then I undid step six. The cartoon person in the diagram does not have to deal with this. The cartoon person never goes back.

I congratulated a woman on her pregnancy. She was not pregnant. The next twelve seconds were the longest twelve seconds of my adult life. She said, very kindly, 'I'm not, but thank you for noticing my new top, which is admittedly quite voluminous.' The grace with which she handled it has haunted me for years. I would not have been so generous. I would have buried me in the garden. She, however, sent me a Christmas card the following December. I am unworthy of her, and I know it.

I put a pound coin in the trolley to release it from its long chain of identical brothers. At that moment I was bound to the trolley by an economic contract. That trolley was mine. I was responsible for it. The relief, at the end of the shop, of slotting it back and reclaiming my pound, is one of the purest emotions available to a modern adult, and I am not ashamed to say I look forward to it more than I look forward to most of the shopping itself.

The wedding had a photo booth, which is a small fabric box designed to extract the dignity of every guest in a strictly time-limited fashion. By the end of the night, the photo album contained one hundred images of grown adults wearing oversized novelty sunglasses and feather boas, pulling faces, holding cardboard signs that said things like 'Team Bride'. We are, all of us, professionals. We have mortgages. The photo booth does not care, and frankly neither did we, by then.

I phoned the internet provider, and a calm voice walked me through a series of steps. Unplug the router. Wait thirty seconds. The thirty seconds, spent in silence, holding a phone, staring at a switched-off box, felt like a small enforced meditation. Plug it back in. And then we waited together, the calm voice and I, watching the lights, hoping, two strangers united in the universal human prayer that the little box would, this time, decide to work.

I went for a beginner's run. Two minutes in, my lungs filed a class-action lawsuit on behalf of every internal organ. Four minutes in, my knees joined the suit as plaintiffs. Six minutes in, a small dog overtook me. The dog was on a lead. The lead was being held by a six-year-old. I made eye contact with the six-year-old. She gave me a thumbs up. I have not run since.

subtopic: trying to take a group photo
sentence: We took the group photo with my phone, and then a chorus rose up: 'take one on mine too'. And so I took it on the next phone. And the next. And the next. I have now photographed the same eight people, in the same pose, eleven times, on eleven devices, and the eight people have held the smile across all eleven, the smile slowly dying, becoming a grimace, becoming a plea. The photo exists eleven times now. It exists too many times. It is everywhere.

The receipt confirmation email arrived in my inbox before I had finished the transaction. It thanked me for my purchase of a single can of dog food, total cost forty-two pounds. I do not have a dog. The dog food was not in my basket. I phoned the supermarket. They told me the system was experiencing some difficulties and that I should treat any emails I received as 'aspirational'. I have framed this advice. I think about it every day.

subtopic: learning a language as an adult
sentence: I have been learning French for eight months using an app, and I am now extremely confident in exactly four areas: I can tell you that the cat is on the table, I can express that I would like a coffee, I can announce that it is raining, and I can declare, with great fluency, that the boy is sad. Whether I will ever stand in a Parisian café and need all four of these facts to be simultaneously true, I do not know. I am prepared, regardless.

The booth printed my four photographs and I examined them in the harsh light outside, hoping that perhaps one of the four would be acceptable, would be the one good one. They are identical. Of course they are identical. They were taken half a second apart. But I keep examining them, as if photo three might, on closer inspection, reveal a hidden charm, a secret dignity, that photos one, two, and four lack. They will not. They are four windows onto the same small disaster.

I bought a saw. I used the saw exactly once. I now own a fence section that is slightly the wrong size, a piece of wood I do not know what to do with, and a small cut on my thumb that has, in the intervening months, achieved iconic status in family folklore. The saw lives in the shed. I am not allowed to touch it again without supervision. I do not contest this. The supervision is, frankly, reassuring.

I confidently told my partner that I did not need the instructions, that the desk was 'intuitive', that I would simply assemble it through reason and common sense. The desk is now a structure that defies the known principles of furniture. It has an asymmetry that cannot be explained. One drawer opens into another drawer. My partner has not said anything. My partner has simply placed the discarded instruction booklet, smoothed flat, on the floor beside me, and left the room.

I asked the AI to refactor my function and it added six new dependencies, deleted my tests, and renamed everything in German. The PR description was a sonnet. The senior engineer who reviewed it just typed 'no' and went home. I respect both of them, in different ways, for entirely different reasons, and I am still trying to undo the German.

The hotel pool was photographed, on the website, as a shimmering turquoise oasis lined with palm trees and serenity. The hotel pool, in reality, was a small rectangle of cold water located beside the car park, surrounded by white plastic chairs, and overlooked by every bedroom window in the building. Swimming in it felt less like a holiday and more like a public audition. I did one length. Everyone watched. I have retired from swimming.

My internet connection faltered during the video call, and so my face froze, mid-sentence, in an expression I had not chosen and would never have chosen, a strange, distorted, half-formed grimace, held aloft for all my colleagues to contemplate for a full eleven seconds. When the connection returned, nobody mentioned it. But they had seen it. The frozen face is out there now, lodged in eleven memories, and there is nothing, ever, that I can do about it.

My code has two states: working, and 'I haven't found the bug yet'. There is no third state. The 'finished' state is a myth promoted by project managers to keep developers compliant, much like the famed 'last sprint' before launch, which has historically been followed by between eleven and forty-seven additional 'last sprints' depending on the size of the company.

I watched a chef on television debone a fish in eleven seconds with a single fluid, balletic motion, and I thought, with the unearned confidence of a man on a sofa, 'I could do that'. I could not do that. I have just spent forty minutes attacking a fish with a knife, and the fish has, somehow, won. There is fish in places fish should not be. The kitchen looks like a crime scene. The chef on television is a trained professional. I am a man who watched a man.

My bio currently says, 'I make excellent toast'. This is true. This is also, somehow, the only line about my personality I can write without dying inside a little. Every attempt at a witty self-summary makes me sound either desperately upbeat or like a hostage. The toast line has attracted exactly one match, a man with no photos, who messaged, 'What kind of toast?' I am marrying him next April.

There is a difficult moment, near the end of the haircut, when the conversation has run its natural course. We have done the holidays. We have done the weather. We have done the weekend. And there is still ten minutes of cutting left, ten minutes of silence to fill, and we both feel it arriving, the conversational drought, and we both reach, desperately, for a new topic, and one of us says, 'busy in here today?', and we are saved, for now.

My partner does not use the snooze button. My partner's alarm goes off once, and my partner simply rises, like a normal, functioning member of society, with no negotiation, no drama, no internal civil war. I watch this happen, from my own side of the bed, through one barely-open eye, with the bewildered awe of a person observing a magic trick. It is the single most impressive thing my partner does, and my partner does not even know it is impressive.

Every family meal abroad turns into a forty-five minute discussion about whether the local cuisine is suitable for my father, whose stomach has, since 1987, refused to accept anything more adventurous than a baked potato. We have toured Greece, Italy, and Spain, and my father has eaten, in each, a remarkably consistent menu of bread, plain pasta, and chips. He has, however, photographed every meal he refused to eat, for the album. The album is now twelve volumes long.

I bought a desk online described as 'easy to assemble' and shown in a photograph being built, effortlessly, by a smiling woman holding a single small tool. The box that arrived contained two hundred and fourteen components, a wordless instruction manual that appeared to have been translated by a fax machine, and a tiny metal key for a process that is never explained. The smiling woman, wherever she is, lied to me, and I think about her often.

I asked the garden centre assistant whether a particular shrub would survive in my garden. She asked about my soil. I did not know. She asked about my light levels. I did not know. She asked which way my garden faced. I confidently said 'outwards'. She closed her eyes for a moment, the way professionals do, and then sold me a cactus, which she described as 'the only thing you cannot meaningfully harm'. I appreciated her honesty. The cactus and I are doing fine.

I told my wife she was drawing her eyebrows too high. She looked surprised. I haven't seen her since, which is fair, because apparently that joke has been making the rounds since the Pleistocene. The eyebrows, however, remain at full mast wherever she is. They have a life of their own now. I just hope they're happy.

I tried to return an item, and the returns process required me to print a label. I do not own a printer. Nobody under the age of fifty owns a printer. I went to a friend's house to use her printer, which was out of ink, then to a library, which had a printer but a queue, then to a shop that charged me more to print the label than the item itself had cost. The jumper, which did not fit, is now mine forever. We have made peace.

There is a man in the gym locker room who conducts his entire post-workout routine in a state of complete, confident nudity, towel slung casually over his shoulder rather than deployed in any useful capacity. He chats. He browses his phone. He discusses, at length, the football. The rest of us perform a careful, fully-clothed ballet of avoidance, changing at impossible angles, while he stands among us, serene, free, a man entirely at peace with himself, and with everyone else's discomfort.

We rented a cottage in Cornwall for a week. The cottage had eight beds, two showers, and one tiny kitchen, and we crammed eleven adults and four children into it. By day four, three couples were quietly considering separation, my brother-in-law had taken to drinking his coffee at the bus stop just to be alone, and the four-year-old had bitten the eight-year-old over a Lego dispute. We have already booked it again for next summer. We learn nothing.

subtopic: first day at a new job
sentence: I spent my entire first day in a state of intense, performed competence, nodding thoughtfully at information I did not understand, taking detailed notes on a process I could not follow, and saying 'great, makes sense' a great many times. It does not make sense. None of it makes sense. But the new job does not know that yet, and I intend to keep it that way for as long as I possibly can, ideally several months.

My toddler ate three crayons today and is now drawing inside herself, which I'm told is technically art. The pediatrician was unimpressed and gave me the kind of look that suggested she sees this exact scenario weekly. I asked if there was anything to worry about. She said only the cost of replacement crayons, which I considered, on reflection, to be a fair joke.

The wedding ceremony was outdoors, in a field, in June, which the couple described in the invitation as 'romantic' and which the weather described as 'an opportunity'. It rained from a clear sky out of pure spite. One hundred guests sat on hay bales under a borrowed assortment of umbrellas, watching the couple exchange vows while a marquee, somewhere behind us, made the sound of a ship in distress. It was, everyone agreed afterwards, the best wedding they had ever attended.

The bug was reported at 4:55 on a Friday. By 4:57, three engineers had pasted it into Slack with the words 'this is interesting'. By 5:02, it had been escalated to staff-level. By 5:15, somebody had filed a JIRA ticket and immediately gone home for the weekend, leaving the rest of us trapped in a meeting that nobody had agreed to be in.

When a plant of mine begins to droop, I do not immediately reach for water or fertiliser. First, I have a word with it. I ask it, gently, what is wrong. I wait, as though a leafy green creature might, given time and a safe space, articulate its needs. The plant never answers. The plant cannot answer. But I feel that the conversation has been had, that the plant has been heard, and then I water it, which was, of course, the actual solution all along.

subtopic: first day at a new job
sentence: I went home after my first day at the new job utterly, profoundly exhausted, despite having, by any objective measure, achieved almost nothing. I had filled in some forms. I had been shown a printer. I had eaten a sandwich anxiously. And yet I was as tired as if I had dug a trench, because the real work of a first day is not work at all, it is the relentless, full-body effort of being new, and being new is the most tiring job there is.

The hairdresser, near the end, picked up a small can and asked, 'do you want some product in it?'. I never know what to say to this. I do not know what 'product' is. I do not know what it does. I have a vision of leaving the salon, getting rained on, and the product running down my face like a melting candle. But saying no feels like a rejection, like declining a gift, and so I said yes, and now my hair is crunchy, and I am afraid to touch it.

I went to the supermarket for three items and took a trolley anyway, telling myself I would only use a small corner of it. I now own forty items. The trolley is full. The trolley was not a container, it turns out. The trolley was an invitation, a vast steel suggestion, a question the supermarket asks you, which is, 'what if you bought all of this?', and to which I, weak and suggestible, answered 'yes, alright then'.

I went for my routine eye test and the optician informed me, with great cheerfulness, that I have entered the stage of life where reading glasses are non-negotiable. I asked what stage that was. She said, 'middle age, sir.' I have not had time to process this. I am sixty-one years old. Middle age was supposed to be over by now. I am, apparently, still in it. Possibly forever. The optician has changed my plans entirely.

I went to the gym for the first time in two years yesterday. The instructor asked what my goals were and I said, with what I thought was disarming honesty, 'survive this hour'. She did not laugh. She put me on something called the assault bike, which is named, I now realise, after what it does to your soul.

subtopic: first day at a new job
sentence: On my first day, a friendly colleague offered to take me for a coffee and 'show me the ropes'. The ropes, it emerged, were primarily a forty-minute briefing on office politics: who to trust, who to avoid, whose stapler not to borrow, and the full, complex backstory of a feud between two departments that began, apparently, over a Christmas party in 2016. I have learned nothing about my actual job. I have learned everything about the war.

The gym locker room benches are exactly the wrong width, too narrow to comfortably sit on, too wide to easily reach over. Every person in the room is engaged in the same awkward struggle: balancing precariously on the edge of a bench while attempting to put on a sock, a task that requires standing on one leg, which the bench actively prevents. We hop. We wobble. We grab at lockers for support. The locker room is, daily, a small uncoordinated festival of grown adults losing their balance.

We bought a small device, a little tag, that you attach to things so they can never be lost, and we attached it to the remote, triumphant, certain we had solved the ancient problem forever. The remote, however, is no longer lost. The little tag's own remote, the thing that finds the thing, is now lost. We have simply moved the problem one step along, and the new lost object is smaller, and harder to find, and we are, if anything, worse off than before.

subtopic: trying to take a group photo
sentence: I suggested we take a 'natural, candid' group photo, where everyone is just laughing and being themselves, rather than a stiff posed one. So I told everyone to 'just laugh naturally'. Nobody can laugh naturally on command. The resulting photograph shows nine people performing the physical act of laughter while their eyes contain nothing but fear and confusion. It is the least natural image ever captured. We look like a group of strangers being held against our will.

I have developed strong opinions about hose attachments. The ratcheting connector is, in my view, superior to the snap-on connector, although the snap-on is more convenient for the casual user. I have, in the past, attempted to share these views at dinner parties. My wife now squeezes my knee, gently, under the table, when I begin. The signal is unmistakable. I have, on occasion, ignored it. The dinner parties have, occasionally, suffered as a result.

I attended a video call from my sofa, dressed, as is now traditional, in a perfectly respectable shirt and a pair of pyjama bottoms that the camera would never see. The call proceeded smoothly until I needed to fetch a document, and forgot, in the moment, the precise nature of my lower half, and stood up, and walked across the room, fully visible, my professional top and my disgraceful bottom both on display, and the meeting, I noticed, went very quiet.

The wifi network in my house has a name that I chose, years ago, in a moment of misplaced humour, and I am now stuck with it forever. Every guest who visits, every repair person, every delivery driver who needs the code, must first read that name aloud, and look at me, and I must explain the joke, which was never very good, and which has aged, frankly, into something I would rather not be associated with at all.

I now own seven different jackets, none of which are appropriate for any specific kind of weather. There is the jacket for slightly damp Saturdays. There is the jacket for mowing. There is the jacket for the school run that I wear over the pyjamas, hoping nobody will notice. There is the jacket I bought because it had a small pocket for a phone, despite already owning four other jackets with phone pockets. My wife has, gently, suggested a wardrobe audit. I have, gently, refused.

I now require approximately ninety minutes of mental preparation to drive in the dark. I have to check the route. I have to consider the weather. I have to confirm that the destination is open. I have to inspect my reading glasses. I have to bring a flask. I have to inform somebody of my route, in case of incident. I have to consider whether the journey could be postponed until the morning. The journey, in question, is to the local Tesco, three miles away.

The remote has been missing for so long now that we have, as a family, simply begun to adapt. We have learned to operate the television via the small, awkward buttons on its underside, a clumsy fumbling ritual performed kneeling on the carpet. We have lowered our expectations. We watch whatever channel the television was on when the remote vanished. We have built an entire new way of life around the loss, and honestly, we are managing.

subtopic: learning a language as an adult
sentence: My Italian teacher asked me to introduce myself to the class. I had prepared. I stood, I said my name, my age, my profession, and then, reaching the end of my prepared material with thirty seconds of attention still trained on me, I panicked and announced, in confident Italian, that I had four sisters. I do not have four sisters. I have no sisters. I now have a relationship with this class built entirely on a foundation of imaginary siblings I will have to maintain for a year.

Dogs greet you as if you have just returned from a six-month deployment, even if you have only been to the bin. Cats greet you as if you have just walked into a private members' club where they are the senior partner and you have neglected to sign in. Both responses are objectively unreasonable. Both responses are also exactly why we have them, and the day they stop is the day I will know something is wrong.

The moon called. It said it was tired of being a satellite and wanted to try something new. I suggested freelance graphic design, and it told me it had no hands. We sat with that in silence for a while. Eventually I offered to be its career coach for a modest fee, and it agreed, on the condition that all our meetings happen at night.

The phrase 'in my day' has, against my own intentions, started slipping into my conversations with increasing frequency. I have caught myself complaining about pop music, the price of stamps, and the fact that nobody knows how to write a proper letter any more. I am, by every available metric, becoming my own father. The transformation is irreversible. My wife finds this both charming and alarming, often within the same sentence.

I took my dog to a behavioural specialist because she had developed a habit of barking at the toaster. The specialist asked thoughtful questions, took notes, observed her for forty minutes, and concluded that my dog hated the toaster. The fee was a hundred and twenty pounds. I could, I think, have arrived at this diagnosis through quiet personal reflection. The dog and the toaster remain locked in their cold war. The toaster has not yet retaliated.

I have, over the years, developed what my wife calls 'the dad nap'. It can occur on any sofa, in any chair, at any hour after 2 p.m. on a weekend. It requires no announcement. It is brief, dignified, and, by all accounts, audible from the next room. The dad nap is the final form of paternal energy storage, and I have come into mine fully. The grandchildren will not see it. They will only see the man who emerges from it, suddenly alert, asking who took the last biscuit.

I bought a gym membership and went exactly once. The trainer asked what my goals were. I said, 'cardiovascular survival into my forties'. She laughed, which I found patronising, until I realised I was already winded just from walking to the rowing machine. The rowing machine has now seen more of me than my dentist has. I do not return its calls.

I have given all of my houseplants names, and I am not going to apologise for it. There is Susan, who is dramatic and droops at the slightest provocation. There is Gerald, who is steady, reliable, and asks for nothing. There is a small succulent called The Intern, who I am not sure has a future here. I talk to them. They do not talk back, which is, frankly, one of the main reasons I prefer them to most of my colleagues.

I made a pencil with two erasers once. It was pointless. My son physically left the country shortly after I told this joke at his graduation. I do not know where he is. I have, however, just thought of three more for his wedding, whenever that happens, and I will deliver them with full enthusiasm, ideally over a microphone, while wearing a slightly bad suit.

I baked bread. The internet promised a golden, crusty loaf with an open, airy crumb. What emerged from my oven was a small, dense, beige sphere with the structural properties of a cricket ball and the weight of a planet. I knocked on the bottom of it, as instructed, to check if it was done. It made the sound of a door. I have, in a sense, baked a small piece of furniture, and I am going to eat it, because I am not made of money.

Every weekend I tell myself I am going to do meal prep. Every weekend I buy the containers. Every weekend I buy the vegetables. Every Sunday evening, I order a pizza, look at the containers and the vegetables, feel a small private shame, and put the containers away clean. The vegetables remain in the fridge for six days before becoming a different, sadder set of vegetables, which I then also do not cook.

Why do recipes always say 'one onion, finely chopped' as if this is a casual ask. It takes me forty minutes and three tea breaks to finely chop a single onion. By the end, I am crying, the cat has fled the room, and the onion is approximately the same level of chopped-ness as when I started. Cookbooks need to be honest about this. I would like a small chapter at the start called 'how long this will actually take', written in tears.

Someone in the office finishes the milk and returns the empty carton to the fridge. They do this every time. They are among us. They walk past us in the corridor, they attend the same meetings, they say good morning, and then, when no one is watching, they place an empty milk carton back on the shelf as if it still has purpose. I have made coffee with no milk so many times that I have, frankly, started to acquire a taste for despair.

subtopic: first day at a new job
sentence: By the end of my first day, I had attended three meetings, the purpose of which I did not understand, about projects I had never heard of, involving people whose roles remained a mystery to me. I sat in each one, nodding, occasionally writing a word down to seem engaged. The word I wrote most often was 'synergy', because everyone else kept saying it, and I have decided that if I say it too, eventually, with enough confidence, I will become a real employee.

The router sits in the hallway, an ugly black box bristling with antennae, and I have spent considerable effort trying to hide it: behind a plant, inside a basket, in a decorative box. But every time I conceal it, the signal weakens, because the router, it seems, needs to be seen, needs to breathe, needs to stand proudly in the open like a small king. And so it remains, on display, the least attractive object in the house, ruling over us all.

I waved at someone across the street thinking it was an old friend. It was not an old friend. It was a stranger. The stranger waved back, looking confused. I committed to the bit. I crossed the road. We had a brief, polite conversation about nothing. I asked after his family. He has a family. I shook his hand. I am not sure he ever realised I did not know him. We exchanged numbers. I am terrified of what happens next.

Microwave meal packaging is the only thing that lies to me with such consistency that I have come to rely on it. The picture on the front shows a generously plated dish, three large prawns, an arrangement of fresh herbs, and a sun-drenched lemon wedge. The actual contents, post-microwave, are a small grey paste, one prawn approximately the size of a fingernail, and a deep philosophical resignation about modern food production.

The recipe said to bake the cake until a skewer 'comes out clean'. I inserted a skewer. It came out clean. I removed the cake, confident, triumphant. The cake was raw in the centre. The skewer had lied. The skewer and the recipe had conspired against me. I now bake everything for an additional, defensive twenty minutes regardless of instructions, and my cakes are dry, and my trust in cutlery is, I think, permanently broken.

My passenger, an old-fashioned soul, brought a paper map. I scoffed. I had the app. The app knew everything. And then, deep in a valley, the phone signal vanished, and the app's confident blue dot froze, stranded, lost, blinking helplessly in a grey void. And my passenger, calm, unhurried, unfolded the paper map across her knees, found us with one finger, and navigated us out by the ancient art of looking at where things actually were. I have not scoffed since.

I attempted to ice a cake smoothly. I had a small flat tool, and I had watched a calm professional glide it around a cake until the surface gleamed. My attempt produced a cake that looked as though the icing had been applied during an earthquake, by a stranger, in the dark. There are peaks. There are valleys. There is one area I have simply covered with a strategically placed strawberry. The strawberry is not decoration. The strawberry is hiding something.

My cat has decided that the most comfortable place in the house is the keyboard of my laptop while I am trying to file my tax return. He has now contributed a number of his own characters to the document, and HMRC may, very shortly, receive a tax return that includes the sequence 'aaaaaaaaaalkjsd;;;;;;;;'. I am not removing it. I want to see what happens. We are in this together now.

There is a specific, beautiful, doomed moment, perhaps four snoozes deep, when I open one eye, look at the time, and perform a desperate piece of mental arithmetic: if I skip breakfast, and skip the shower, and run, I can still snooze once more. The maths is always wrong. The maths is always optimistic. But I do the maths anyway, every morning, my half-asleep brain conjuring a fantasy timeline in which everything goes perfectly and I am not late.

I now understand why my mother used to lock herself in the bathroom and pretend she couldn't hear us. I previously considered this behaviour deeply unfair. I now consider it the foundational survival skill of parenthood. I have my own bathroom now. I am in it more than I would like to admit. The Wi-Fi reaches in here, which is, frankly, the only home improvement I deeply care about.

Every printout that emerges from the office printer carries, somewhere on the page, a faint grey streak, a ghostly vertical line, a small permanent flaw. We have all noticed it. Nobody has fixed it. We have collectively decided that the streak is fine, that it is, in fact, simply a feature of all documents now, and that any document arriving without the streak would, frankly, look suspicious, look fake, look like it came from somewhere better than here.

I assembled a wardrobe over the weekend. Eleven hours of my life are gone. The wardrobe stands. It is, technically, a wardrobe. There is, however, one shelf that goes diagonally for reasons I cannot explain. There are also four screws I do not know what to do with. The instructions, in twelve languages, do not mention these screws. My wife says, 'we are leaving the screws in the kitchen drawer for now.' We are leaving the screws in the kitchen drawer forever.

I am in a step competition with my brother, mediated entirely by our fitness trackers, and it has destroyed my relationship with the outdoors. I no longer go for walks. I go on missions. I pace the platform at the train station. I take the long way to the bin. Last Sunday I walked in circles around my own kitchen island for half an hour while a documentary played, purely to overtake him before midnight. He won anyway. He has a dog.

I typed my password, confidently, and the website rejected it. I typed it again, more carefully, certain I had simply mistyped. Rejected. I typed it a third time, slowly, deliberately, treating each character as precious. Rejected. And then came the cold, creeping horror, the realisation that the password in my head, the password I trusted, the password I have used for years, is simply, somehow, no longer the password, and I do not know when it stopped being the password, or what it is now.

I own a plant that the shop described as 'unkillable'. I have killed it. Twice. I have bought the same unkillable plant on two separate occasions and reduced each one, through no intentional effort, to a small brown reminder of my own limitations. The shop assistant, on my third visit, did not say anything. He simply handed me a plastic plant, gently, with the look of a man releasing a bird that cannot fly. The plastic plant is thriving. I water it anyway.

I laid out all the furniture pieces on the living room floor in neat, organised rows, the way a confident person would, the way a person in control would. I counted the screws. I identified the panels. And then I began, and within twenty minutes the neat rows were gone, the floor was chaos, and I was holding a wooden dowel and a hex key and a piece labelled 'F', and I could not, for the life of me, locate piece 'A', the foundation, the beginning of everything.

There is a particular art to entering a building with a wet umbrella, an art I have never mastered. I arrive, dripping, and stand in the doorway, performing a complex and clumsy procedure: shaking the umbrella, which sprays everyone nearby, then trying to collapse it, which traps my hand, then looking, desperately, for the special umbrella stand that the building never, ever has. I end up carrying the wet umbrella around with me all day, leaving a small, sad trail.

The Tannoy on the platform announced, in cheerful tones, that the next train would be the 8:14 to Hove, calling at every station between here and the end of human patience. I was waiting for the 8:11 to London. I checked the board. The 8:11 was, according to the board, on time. The 8:11 did not exist. It had never existed. I had imagined the entire train. I went home. I am working from the kitchen table. I am writing this from the kitchen table.

The neighbourhood group chat began, three years ago, as a sensible forum for reporting suspicious activity and lost cats. It is now, primarily, a stage for one man, Derek, who posts daily updates on the activity of a fox. The fox has crossed the road. The fox has been near the bins. The fox, this morning, 'gave Derek a look'. Forty-seven adults receive these notifications. Nobody asked for them. Nobody can leave. We are all hostages of Derek and the fox.

I bought a plant labelled 'low maintenance, ideal for beginners'. The plant was dead within nine days. I returned to the garden centre, holding the brown remains aloft like evidence, and the assistant looked at it, looked at me, and said, very gently, 'what did you do to it?' I had watered it. That was, apparently, the crime. There is, it seems, a plant so low-maintenance that the act of caring for it constitutes abuse, and I had bought it.

Every man on this app is either six foot four, owns a fish he is holding aloft like a trophy, or is currently 'between things'. I am not entirely sure what 'between things' means, but I suspect it covers a multitude of personal situations including bankruptcy, recent divorce, and a deep ongoing argument with his housemate. I have started swiping on the fish instead. The fish has more clarity of purpose.

Someone said, 'enjoy your meal,' and I said, 'you too.' The waiter does not need to enjoy my meal. The waiter is not eating my meal. The waiter has, in fact, eaten his own meal hours ago. He looked at me with the gentle pity of a man who has heard this before. I considered correcting myself. I did not. I committed to the social error and ate my entire dinner in shame. I have, to this day, never returned to that restaurant.

I went to the hairdresser and, when asked what I wanted, I gestured vaguely at my own head and said 'just, you know, a tidy-up, neaten it'. This is not instruction. This is not information. I have given the hairdresser nothing, a void, a shrug, and now they must guess, must read my soul, must intuit from my general energy what a person like me deserves. They did their best. The result is fine. It is always fine. 'Fine' is the natural outcome of communicating with a shrug.

The passport photo booth is a small fabric cubicle of judgement. You sit on a stool that cannot be adjusted to any human height. A disembodied voice tells you to look at the camera. A green light promises a photo, then a flash arrives several seconds later, capturing not your prepared face but your true face, the face of a person waiting, uncertain, slightly afraid. That face is now my legal identity. That face will be scrutinised by border officials worldwide.

subtopic: humour about work, tech, or science
sentence: Schrödinger's cat is in a box and may be either alive or dead. My inbox is a box and definitely contains both an unread email from my manager and the will to live, in superposition. The act of opening either one will collapse the wavefunction in a way I am not emotionally prepared for. So I leave both unobserved, scientifically speaking, and the universe holds its breath.

Children are an excellent investment, if your goal is being interrupted approximately seven hundred times during the only good film you have rented in a year. I have watched the first ten minutes of every prestige drama released since 2019. I have not seen the middle of any of them. I do not know what happens. I will go to my grave unsure whether anyone in any of these series ever actually solved anything.

The personal trainer at my gym is twenty-three years old, has the body fat percentage of a particularly disciplined seabird, and refers to his clients as 'champ' in a tone that suggests he is unsure of all our names. He told me I had great potential, which is the polite trainer phrase for 'we are starting from the absolute bottom'. I will be billing him for the emotional honesty next week.

I attempted to install a smart doorbell. The smart doorbell is now connected to my neighbour's Wi-Fi. The neighbour and I have not discussed this. The neighbour is getting notifications every time my postman approaches my house. I have decided to leave it as it is. The neighbour, by all evidence, finds it charming. He has begun sending me brief reports of my own deliveries. I will not be returning the smart doorbell.

I told my friend a joke about UDP. I'm not sure if he got it. That joke depends on you understanding UDP, a network protocol famous for not confirming whether the message arrived. If you understood the joke, congratulations, you are a horrible person. If you didn't, please continue to live your life unburdened by this knowledge. It will serve you better than it has served me.

Why did the man drop his ice cream? Because he was hit by a bus. That's the joke. It is not a good joke. It does, however, illustrate a useful principle, which is that not all setups deserve a clever payoff, and not all suffering is meaningful. Sometimes a man just loses his ice cream, and the universe shrugs. The ice cream cone, for what it's worth, ended up on the pavement.

My father insists, every year, that he does not need a map. My father has, every year, ended up at a roundabout he does not recognise, in a town we did not intend to visit, while my mother quietly says, 'I told you to take the third exit, John.' He never takes the third exit. He has never, in fifty-three years of marriage, taken the third exit. The third exit is, by now, a metaphor for everything.

The hotel room had a complicated panel of light switches by the door, none of them labelled. Over the course of one evening I turned on a light in the bathroom, a light I never located, a fan somewhere in the walls, and, on one memorable occasion, the television in the room next door. I gave up and lived by the glow of my phone for three nights, like a Victorian, but with worse posture and a charging cable.

I own, at any given time, either zero umbrellas or seven umbrellas, and there is no stable middle state. On a sunny day I will discover four umbrellas in my hallway and wonder where they all came from. On a rainy day, the same hallway will be, mysteriously, entirely umbrella-free, every single one of them having quietly slipped away to wherever umbrellas go, leaving me to face the weather with nothing but a newspaper and regret.

I left one pair of shoes in an online basket and closed the tab. I have since been pursued across the entire internet by those shoes. They appear beside news articles. They appear inside videos. They appeared, last night, in an advert during a programme about medieval cathedrals, which felt like a stretch even for them. The shoes will not let me go. I am beginning to think the only way to be free of the shoes is to buy the shoes, which is, of course, exactly the plan.

I tried to learn the guitar during lockdown, like everyone else. Five years later, I can play a strangled approximation of Wonderwall, and that's it. My neighbours have offered, very politely, to buy the guitar from me at any price. I have declined, because the guitar and I are working through some things together, and a sale would feel like abandonment.

subtopic: trying to take a group photo
sentence: We asked a kind passing stranger to take a photo of our whole group in front of the famous landmark. The stranger, full of goodwill, took the phone, stepped back, and then took eleven photographs of, primarily, our knees. The landmark is not in any of them. Half the group is not in any of them. But we thanked the stranger warmly, because they had tried, and you cannot tell a kind stranger that they have photographed your knees. You simply keep the knee photos. Forever.

A friend of mine claims he can communicate with vegetables. He says he speaks fluent cabbage, decent broccoli, and only kitchen-Spanish levels of leek. I asked him what the carrots had to say and he told me, with a completely straight face, that root vegetables are mostly into politics, and they are extremely opinionated about parsnips.

On the cooking show, the host always has a small bowl of every ingredient, pre-measured, pre-chopped, lined up in a beautiful row, ready to go. They call this 'mise en place'. They do not show you who chopped all of those things. They do not show you the forty minutes of weeping over onions. The bowls simply exist, perfect and prepared, and I, watching, believed that cooking was the easy part, the part with the bowls. It is not. The bowls are everything. The bowls are a lie.

At the end of the video call, the host said the dreaded words: 'any questions before we wrap up?'. The screen filled with silence. Twelve faces stared back, each one performing a small theatre of thoughtfulness, each one praying nobody would speak, because a question now would cost everyone another ten minutes. The silence held. We had, collectively, willed the meeting to end, and our shared, desperate quiet was, in its way, the most unified the team had ever been.

I tried to make macarons because a television programme made it look like a charming afternoon activity. Macarons, I have since discovered, are not a charming afternoon activity. Macarons are a test of the human spirit. My first batch cracked. My second batch was hollow. My third batch fused into a single continental macaron the size of a dinner plate. I have decided that macarons are not food. Macarons are a hazing ritual, and I have failed to be hazed.

I went in for a handshake. He went in for a hug. We met somewhere in the middle in a kind of partial collision involving an elbow to my chest, a half-pat on my shoulder, and a confused noise I am not sure either of us has heard our own throats produce before. We are now colleagues. We see each other every Wednesday. We do not greet each other any more. We just nod, professionally, like two combat veterans who have agreed never to discuss the incident.

Why do programmers prefer dark mode? Because light attracts bugs. I told this to my dentist, who, I now realise, is not a programmer, and has very limited patience for puns delivered at full volume with a mouth full of suction tube. She did not laugh. She did, however, drill deeper than I think was strictly necessary on the tooth in question.

What's the difference between a duck? One of its legs is both the same. That sentence has been broken by design, and I will not be repairing it. If you have a strong urge to fix the grammar, please direct that energy into something more useful, like writing a will, or finally calling your mother, both of which you have been putting off for entirely too long.

The car was packed at six in the morning. By 7:45 we had unpacked the car twice to look for a passport that turned out to be in my mother's coat pocket all along. We left at 9:13, an hour and a half behind schedule, with everyone slightly furious at each other and the youngest child crying because somebody had said the wrong word, very quietly, two miles back. The holiday had begun. We were already exhausted.

There is a specific peril in the hairdresser's chair, which is that you are facing a large mirror, watching yourself being spoken to, and you must respond to the conversation while also pretending not to be staring directly at your own slowly-emerging haircut. I do not know where to look. If I look at the hairdresser, I have to twist my head, which they dislike. If I look at the mirror, I am looking at myself, vainly. I have settled, throughout, on looking at a poster about conditioner.

At the end of the transaction, the machine asked me to rate my self-checkout experience by pressing one of four faces, ranging from a beaming smile to a face of profound sorrow. I had just spent six minutes being accused of theft by a robot. I pressed the sad face firmly. The machine thanked me, brightly, for my feedback, and I understood, in that moment, that the feedback goes nowhere, helps no one, and exists purely so the machine can feel it has listened.

The login screen offered me a choice: enter my password, or answer a 'security question'. The security question was 'what was the name of your first pet?'. I have, in my life, given several different answers to this question across several different websites, in several different moods, and I no longer know which lie I told where. My first pet has, through my own carelessness, acquired four names, and any of them might be the truth, and the website is waiting.

I have, over many years, become a connoisseur of umbrella failure, and I can now identify, by the sound alone, the precise moment an umbrella gives up. There is a small metallic click, a tiny snap, and then a section of the umbrella simply goes limp, droops, dangles, and from that moment on the umbrella tilts at a permanent jaunty angle, channelling rain directly down the back of my neck, and I know, instantly, that another one has been lost to the cause.

There is a specific category of gym-goer who arrives, opens their locker, sets up an elaborate base camp of toiletries, supplements, and equipment, and then proceeds to spend significantly more time in the locker room than they ever spend in the actual gym. I have watched a man arrange his shelf of products for eleven minutes. I do not know if he ever exercises. I think, for him, the gym is the locker room, and the locker room is a hobby, and the weights are merely an excuse.

The man on the train opposite me has been making a phone call in a foghorn voice for forty-three minutes. He has discussed his dental work, his mother's opinions on his wife, and the precise terms of a contract he is renegotiating. I now know more about his life than I know about most of my own relatives. He has not lowered his voice. We have made eye contact twice. He winked the second time. I may have a new uncle.

I tried to take my own passport photo at home to save money, against a white wall, holding my phone at arm's length. I took, in total, eighty-four photographs. In every single one, I am either blinking, leaning, smiling slightly, casting a shadow, or wearing an expression that the official website firmly describes as 'not acceptable'. I have, somehow, never seen my own face look correct. I went to the booth. The booth captured my wrongness in one efficient flash.

subtopic: learning a language as an adult
sentence: I have been learning Japanese, and the writing system has three separate alphabets, one of which exists, as far as I can tell, purely to humble me. Every time I feel I am making progress, I encounter a new character that looks like a small, complicated house and means something like 'the feeling of mild regret on a Tuesday'. I am not progressing through the language. I am being slowly, gently introduced to the full scale of my own ignorance.

subtopic: trying to take a group photo
sentence: The phone was propped against a water bottle, the timer was set, and I had ten seconds to sprint from the camera into position with the rest of the group. I have done this before. I know the run. But the timer is always faster than a human being, and the resulting photograph captures the group, smiling serenely, and me, a blur at the edge of the frame, mid-leap, my face a mask of pure athletic panic, arriving at the photo a fraction of a second too late.

My grandson tried to show me how to use a new app on my phone. He moved his thumb at a speed that, frankly, was not legally permitted for use on a screen. I asked him to slow down. He slowed down by approximately twelve percent. Three minutes later, I no longer recognised the home screen. I do not know what app I am now in. He has gone home. I am stuck. My phone is, in some sense, no longer mine.

I ordered a single phone charger and it arrived in a cardboard box large enough to relocate a family of badgers. The charger, a small object weighing approximately nothing, sat alone in the centre of this vast space, cushioned by an extravagant amount of paper, like a tiny king in an enormous throne room. I felt the universe was trying to tell me something about scale, and proportion, and the modern world, but mostly I felt I now had a very large empty box and no clear plan.

The television remote has vanished, and so my entire household has now stopped what it was doing and entered a state of full archaeological excavation. Cushions are lifted. Hands are plunged into the dark crevices of the sofa. The search has spread, illogically, to the kitchen, to the bathroom, to rooms the remote has never visited. We could simply press the buttons on the television itself, but nobody will say this, because the remote must be found, on principle, and the principle is sacred.

There are 10 kinds of people in this world: those who understand binary, those who don't, and those who didn't realise this was a joke until somebody explained it to them at a party, ruining the joke and the party simultaneously. I have personally been all three of those people, sometimes within the same conversation.

On a Saturday, with nowhere to be, I will wake naturally, refreshed, at a reasonable hour, my body cheerful and ready. On a Monday, with everything to do, the same body must be dragged from sleep across forty minutes of brutal negotiation. My body knows the difference between the days. My body has read my calendar. And my body has decided, firmly, that it will only cooperate on the days when cooperation does not matter.

The fitness tracker has a feature where it shows you, on a little graph, how you compare to 'people like you'. People like me, apparently, are doing extremely well. People like me are running marathons and climbing things. I do not feel like people like me. I feel like a person who has been mistakenly grouped with the wrong people, and I would like the graph to find me a new, slower, more honest peer group, possibly one that also enjoys sitting down.

subtopic: trying to take a group photo
sentence: The group photo descended into chaos when someone suggested 'a silly one'. We had a perfectly good serious photo. But the silly one had been suggested, and so we had to do the silly one, and the silly one involved everyone pulling a face and one person attempting a small jump. The silly photo took eleven attempts, far more than the serious photo, because being silly on demand is exhausting, and by the end the silliness had curdled into a kind of grim, committed despair.

I sent one single document to the office printer, a single page, and the printer responded by demanding I install a driver, update the firmware, log into an account I did not know I had, and confirm, repeatedly, that I genuinely wished to print. By the time the page emerged, twenty minutes later, I had forgotten what the document was, why I needed it, and, briefly, who I was. The printer had won, as the printer always wins.

Two people on the video call began to speak at exactly the same instant, and then both stopped, and then both said 'sorry, you go', and then both started again, simultaneously, and stopped again. This polite collision repeated four times, a small loop of mutual deference, while the other twelve participants watched in silence, until finally a third person, taking pity, simply talked over both of them, breaking the spell and saving us all.

subtopic: learning a language as an adult
sentence: The language app sends me a notification every evening that begins encouraging and grows, over a missed week, genuinely menacing. It started with 'time for your lesson!'. Then 'don't break your streak!'. Then a small cartoon owl looking, frankly, disappointed in me. Last night the notification simply said 'these reminders don't seem to be working' in a tone of quiet defeat, and I have never felt so seen, or so judged, by a piece of software.

I selected a trolley, tested it for wheel integrity by pushing it back and forth twice in the entrance, declared it sound, and set off. Within eleven seconds, the moment it bore the weight of actual groceries, it revealed its true character: a deafening rattle, a persistent leftward drift, and a single wheel that no longer rotated but merely scraped. The test had been a lie. The trolley had performed wellness. The trolley had deceived me, and I respect its patience.

My fitness tracker detected my heart rate spiking and asked, with concern, if I was doing a workout. I was not doing a workout. I was reading an email from my manager. The tracker, helpfully, offered to start logging the activity. I declined. I do not want a permanent record of how my body responds to the phrase 'quick chat?'. Some metrics are better left uncollected. Some data, once gathered, can never be unknown.

There is an unspoken supermarket law that two people who know each other will, inevitably, leave their trolleys parked end to end across the entire width of an aisle while they catch up. They will discuss a christening. They will discuss a hip operation. And behind them, a quiet queue of polite people forms, nobody willing to say anything, all of us silently aging, waiting for the conversation about the hip to reach its natural conclusion so we can reach the pasta.

My hairdresser asked if I had 'any big plans for the weekend'. I did not. My big plan for the weekend was to do some laundry and possibly tidy a cupboard. I could not say this. So I said, 'oh, just seeing some friends, the usual', which implied a rich and active social life I do not possess. The hairdresser smiled, pleased for me. I have now lied, again, in this chair, and the lies are accumulating, an entire false biography assembled forty minutes at a time.

The cooking show host casually 'flipped' the contents of the pan with a confident flick of the wrist, sending the food up in a graceful arc and catching it perfectly. I tried this. I sent a quantity of stir-fried vegetables directly upwards. Some of them returned to the pan. Most of them did not. Some of them, I believe, are still on the ceiling, in a pattern, like a small green constellation, a permanent monument to my belief in myself.

I have just collected my new passport photos, and the person looking back at me from these images is not a person I recognise or particularly want to be associated with for the next ten years. I am not allowed to smile. I am not allowed to look happy. The official guidance demands a 'neutral expression', and so I appear, in all four photos, like a man who has just been gravely insulted and is choosing, with great difficulty, not to react.

subtopic: learning a language as an adult
sentence: I told my German tutor I wanted to sound more natural. She said the first step was to learn the word for 'um'. Apparently every language has its own specific filler noise, its own particular sound of a person thinking, and using the wrong one marks you instantly as a foreigner. I have now spent two weeks practising the German 'um'. I can do the 'um' perfectly. I cannot do any of the actual sentences, but I can hesitate like a true Berliner.

I returned my trolley to the trolley bay and discovered that the act of slotting it neatly into the line, nesting it perfectly with its fellows, gave me a small and disproportionate sense of accomplishment. In a day otherwise devoid of clear wins, the trolley had clicked into place, the chain had connected, and I had, briefly, completed something. I stood there a moment too long. A man waiting behind me cleared his throat. I had been savouring the trolley. I left.

My yoga teacher keeps saying, 'find your edge'. I have found my edge. My edge is approximately twenty seconds into a downward dog, at which point my arms file a formal complaint with the rest of my body and I lie face-down on the mat pretending to be in a restorative pose. The instructor walks past, nods, and continues. We have an understanding now. The other students assume I am very advanced.

I have a relationship with a delivery driver I have never met. He knows my house. He knows the gate sticks. He knows to leave parcels behind the green bin, not the black one, a distinction I communicated through a series of increasingly elaborate notes taped to the door. We have never spoken. We have never seen each other. He is, by volume of trust placed in him, one of the most significant people in my life, and his name, according to the app, is Dave.

I tried to fix the dripping tap. The internet told me it was a simple matter of replacing the washer. I bought eleven different washers, in case. I dismantled the tap. Water sprayed, in a great fountain, directly upwards into the ceiling. I learned, in that moment, that there is a separate water shut-off valve I should have used first. I have now learned this twice. I do not, evidently, retain plumbing lessons. The tap still drips. The ceiling now has a small stain.

I shared my umbrella with a friend, an act of kindness, and discovered that sharing an umbrella is, in fact, an impossible geometric problem. The umbrella is sized for one. To cover two people, we must walk pressed unnaturally close together, in an awkward, shuffling lockstep, each of us subtly leaning toward the other, and even then, one shoulder of each of us remains permanently in the rain. We did not stay dry. We did, however, become much closer friends.

The hotel breakfast was advertised as a 'continental buffet'. I have now seen the continent in question, and it consists of three croissants under a heat lamp, a yoghurt that expired during a previous administration, and a coffee machine that produces a beige liquid the staff themselves refuse to make eye contact with. A man in a dressing gown took the last croissant ahead of me with the speed of an Olympic sprinter. I respected him. I also will never forgive him.

There is a deep and unspoken law in my household that whoever holds the remote holds the power, and so the remote is never simply set down. It is guarded. It is placed deliberately, on the arm of the chair, beneath a protective hand. To leave the room while holding the remote is to surrender the throne. I have learned to take the remote with me to the kitchen, on principle, a small black sceptre, lest a sibling stage a quiet coup in my absence.

Hello hungry, I'm Dad. I have been doing this since 1994, and I have never once had a child laugh genuinely at it. The performance, however, is not for them. The performance is for me, and for the long unbroken chain of fathers stretching back to the Pleistocene who said the equivalent of this joke and were also met with stony silence at the family fire.

I told a friend, lightly, as a joke, that I talk to my plants, expecting her to laugh. She did not laugh. She told me, in complete seriousness, that she does the same, that she has done it for years, that her monstera is called Clive and that Clive is, in her words, 'a good listener'. And in that moment a great wall fell between us, and we recognised one another, two members of the same quiet, slightly unhinged society, and our friendship deepened immeasurably.

I tried to be polite and held the door open for someone. They were further away than I thought. I waited. They walked slowly. I had committed. They walked more slowly. We made eye contact. There was no going back. They eventually arrived, ten seconds later than would have been comfortable, said 'thanks' with the energy of someone defusing a small bomb, and we both pretended that the door interaction had been perfectly normal. We were both wrong.

The host of the cooking show said, with a relaxed smile, 'and now we just let it rest'. I had never heard food described as needing rest. But I trusted the show, and so my roast chicken rested. It rested for the recommended time. And then, full of confidence, I carved it and served it, and it was, to be fair to the chicken, perfectly fine. The chicken had rested. I, who had cleaned three pans and wept over garlic, had not. There is no segment for the cook's rest.

The wedding invitation said the dress code was 'smart casual', which is the most dangerous phrase in the English language. I arrived in chinos and a blazer, having agonised for an hour. Half the room was in three-piece suits. The other half was in jeans. The groom was in a kilt. Nobody was 'smart casual'. Smart casual does not exist. It is a trap laid by couples to watch their guests suffer, and I fell straight into it, holding a gift-wrapped toaster.
